Notes: Earliest documented Jewish presence (basis of Year Established, c. 35 CE): Encyclopaedia Judaica (Isaiah Gafni) states that in the 1st c. CE 'a large number of Jews took refuge in Seleucia' after the defeat of the Jewish leader Anilaeus (c. 35). Population blank: no count of resident Jews. The same entry says Seleucia (founded by Seleucus I Nicator, 312-280 BCE) was inhabited in the Parthian period mainly by Greeks and Syrians, and cites Pliny's figure of 600,000 inhabitants - a total-population figure for a gentile city, NOT used. Founding of the city (c. 307-300 BCE), Parthian conquest (141 BCE) and the revolt against Parthia/siege by Vardanes (c. 35-42 CE) are not rows because no Jews are documented there before c. 35 CE. A tertiary EBSCO Research Starter (2022) says the Hellenistic city had 'numerous Jews' among its inhabitants, but gives no evidence or date, so it is not treated as documented presence. Jewish Encyclopedia (Anilai) puts the brothers' robber-state c. 18-33 CE, so the flight to Seleucia may be slightly earlier than c. 35.

Josephus, Antiquities 18.9.8 (18.372-373): after the ruin of Anileus's party the Babylonians attacked the Jews, who 'went to Seleucia, the principal city of those parts, which was built by Seleucus Nicator' (inhabited by Macedonians, more Greeks and some Syrians); 'thither did the Jews fly, and lived there five years, without any misfortunes'; in the sixth year a pestilence at Babylon brought more Jewish migrants into Seleucia. Ancient literary attestation of a substantial (refugee) Jewish community living in the city; no resident count. Josephus gives no year; dated c. 35 CE (arrival) following the Encyclopaedia Judaica chronology (Anilaeus defeated c. 35); Scales & Soon (Classical Quarterly 2025/26) place the brothers' rule 'sometime in the 20s-30s c.e.'.

Massacre and end of the community. Josephus, Antiquities 18.9.9 (18.374-379): the quarrelling Greeks and Syrians of Seleucia, after the Jews had helped the Syrians in a sedition, reconciled through 'their common hatred to the Jews' and 'slew about fifty thousand of them; nay, the Jews were all destroyed, excepting a few who escaped' with help of friends or neighbours; the survivors fled to Ctesiphon and then, with most Babylonian Jews, to Neerda (Nehardea) and Nisibis. Population 0 because Josephus states that all the Jews of Seleucia were destroyed except a few who fled the city. The figure of c. 50,000 is an ancient death toll (unverified; Goodblatt 1987 regards Josephus's sequencing of the episodes as secondary) and is NOT used as a population figure. Year c. 40 CE = the 'sixth year' after the c. 35 arrival (approximate; often placed c. 40-41 CE).

Encyclopaedia Judaica (Isaiah Gafni): the Jewish refugees first allied with the Syrians, but the Greek party broke up the alliance; Greeks and Syrians then united in enmity to the Jews and 'in a sudden attack upon the community over 50,000 Jews were said to have been slain'; the surviving Jews eventually fled to Nehardea and Nisibis. Death toll (ancient figure, hedged by the source with 'were said') in Notes only; Population blank. The entry gives no year for the massacre beyond following the c. 35 defeat of Anilaeus; dated c. 40 CE per Josephus's 'sixth year'. (EJ 'Nisibis' entry likewise says Nisibis absorbed the Jews of Seleucia and Ctesiphon who fled their neighbours' vengeance.)

Jewish Encyclopedia (1906, J. Jacobs and S. Ochser), 'Seleucia' no. 2: Babylonian Jews fled to this Parthian city when hard pressed by the Gentile population; the Greeks and Syrians, 'continually quarreling', united out of common hatred of the fugitives and killed 5,000 of them 'about 41 B.C.' (citing Josephus Ant. 18.9.9). The source's date 41 B.C. is evidently an error for c. 41 CE (Josephus places the episode after the Anilaeus affair under Artabanus III), and its 5,000 differs from Josephus's 'about fifty thousand'. Death toll only; Population blank.
